summary.text:
A large, well-run book that made one deliberate bet, and the bet has gone the other way. Northumberland ended 2025-26 with £898.468m of external debt at 3.41% against a CFR of £1,109.778m, leaving £211.310m internal. The average rate came down 0.12% over the year and interest paid finished £6.995m under budget, so the year itself went well.

The bet is at paragraph 15.8. Of the new borrowing taken in the year, £181m was short-term — £116m from other local authorities and £65m from the PWLB — explicitly because of 'the market opinion that the interest rates will fall in future years'. At the year end £116.000m of market and local authority debt sits under one year at 4.22%. Paragraph 15.10 repeats the view: 'current market forecasts indicate that the interest rates will decrease in 2026-27'.

They do not. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the one-year OIS is about 4.11%. Short local authority money has been trading through Bank Rate rather than under it. Alongside that sits £17.000m of LOBOs with call dates in 2026-27, which the report already flags. The refinancing is manageable in a book this size; the point is that it now has to be done into a market that moved against the assumption.

officer.subject: £121m of your PWLB reprices inside two years
officer.body:
Hi Kyle,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit and Standards on 23 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your annual report is unusually well evidenced: the split between cash movement and amortised-cost remeasurement at 15.7 is the kind of thing most reports quietly net off.

Two cross-checks first, so you can see our figures tie to yours. We hold all 84 of your PWLB loans — £559.86m at a weighted 3.13% — which is your Table 1 exactly. And paragraph 10.2 gives the one-year certainty rate at 31 March as approximately 5.04%; our series gives 5.04% for the same day.

The thing we'd flag is the short end. £181m of the year's new borrowing was taken short by design — £116m from other authorities and £65m from the PWLB — and 15.8 is straightforward about the reason: the market opinion that rates would fall. At the year end £116.000m of market and local authority debt sat under twelve months at 4.22%, and on our side £121m of the PWLB book matures inside two years as well.

That view hasn't come good yet. Bank Rate is still 3.75% and the one-year OIS is about 4.11%, so the curve is pricing a rise rather than the fall assumed at 15.10. Short local authority money has been trading around or through Bank Rate rather than under it. In a book of £898m this is a manageable amount of refinancing rather than a problem — but it does now have to be done into a market that went the other way, and the £17.000m of LOBOs with 2026-27 call dates sits alongside it.

Nothing in that needs a meeting or a subscription. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve. Your loan book, priced daily against the DMO repayment curve so premiums and discounts are a lookup rather than a request, is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. And the monthly sector breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is a useful read on how thin the market is before you roll.

On training, three fit where Northumberland is: Interest rate risk, for the short-dated third of the book; LOBO loans, for the calls in this financial year; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
